clue.text: The end of the planet, recorded by

annotationWithheld.why: Clue as held, 'The end of the planet, recorded by (3,5,4)', is cut short: the author after 'recorded by' (apparently 26, Edith Wharton, whose collection bears this title) is missing, so there is no definition.
annotationWithheld.clue: The end of the planet, recorded by

clue.text: Humble admirer of Florence Dombey is that bravura part for Dustin Hoffman

parts.note: Mr Toots is the shy, devoted suitor of Florence in Dickens's Dombey and Son
i.e., id est, is Latin for 'that is'

explanation.surface: A Dickens devotee's name is linked to Dustin Hoffman's star turn.
explanation.walkthrough: Hoffman's celebrated cross-dressing role gave the 1982 film its title; Dickens's bashful Mr Toots supplies the first five letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Hoffman played an actor disguised as a woman in the film of that title, a showpiece role.

clue.text: Outstanding, like Strachey's terminus points

explanation.surface: A remarkable thing is compared to Strachey and a railway station's compass bearings.
explanation.walkthrough: Lytton Strachey's book is Eminent Victorians, and VICTORIANS can be split as VICTORIA (the London rail terminus) plus N and S (compass points), so the terminus points are 'eminent' in his title.
explanation.definitionFit: Distinguished or prominent people stand out above others, and Strachey's biographical subjects were described by that adjective.

clue.text: "And be your today the helmet of Navarre" (Macaulay)

definitions.text: "And be your today the helmet of Navarre" (Macaulay)

parts.words: And be your today the helmet of Navarre" (Macaulay
parts.note: a line from Macaulay's poem Ivry with one word left out: the royal banner Henri of Navarre's men are told to follow

explanation.walkthrough: In Macaulay's Ivry the king's white plume is to serve as the army's battle standard; the missing word is the name of the French sacred banner.
explanation.definitionFit: The ancient red banner of the French kings served as a rallying standard in battle, as the helmet's plume does in the poem.

clue.text: Popular essentials include valued possessions

indicators.note: the words 'Popular essentials' include the answer within them, running across the word break

explanation.surface: Popular must-haves cover the things we treasure most.
explanation.walkthrough: The run sits at the end of 'Popular' and the start of 'essentials'.
explanation.definitionFit: Roman household gods, as in 'lares and penates', came to stand for a family's cherished belongings.

clue.text: Miscellaneous notes on mania out of control

indicators.note: the letters of 'on mania' run wild and are rearranged

explanation.surface: Scattered jottings about a mania that has run riot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out of control' rearranges ONMANIA.
explanation.definitionFit: A collection of jottings on all manner of subjects is a book of odds and ends, from Latin 'omnia', all things.

clue.text: Some revel in a work much admired by Jane Austen

definitions.text: work much admired by Jane Austen

indicators.note: Some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Some readers delight in a novel that Jane Austen loved.
explanation.walkthrough: Fanny Burney's novel of 1778 was a favourite of Austen's.
explanation.definitionFit: Fanny Burney's epistolary novel was praised by Austen, who named it in Northanger Abbey.

clue.text: His imagination was romantic

parts.note: points to the Oxford scholar whose study of the Romantic poets was titled The Romantic Imagination

explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads like a remark on someone's dreamy temperament, but it names the author of the 1949 book The Romantic Imagination.
explanation.definitionFit: The Warden of Wadham College wrote a celebrated critical book on English Romantic poetry with that title.

clue.text: Flying heart doctors

parts.note: winged little cupids who tend to matters of love, pictured as airborne physicians of the heart

explanation.walkthrough: 'heart doctors' suggests cardiologists, but the winged ones meant are little Cupids of Italian art.
explanation.definitionFit: Plump winged love-gods painted in Renaissance art are figures who make people fall in love.

clue.text: Our Edna might compose a formal poem

indicators.note: the letters of 'Our Edna' are composed into a new order

explanation.surface: A woman called Edna might write a strict verse form.
explanation.walkthrough: 'might compose' rearranges OUREDNA.
explanation.definitionFit: A French verse form with a refrain and only two rhymes is a strictly patterned poem.

clue.text: Gorky claimed these seats of learning

explanation.surface: Maxim Gorky staked his claim on places of higher education.
explanation.walkthrough: Gorky's autobiographical trilogy ends with My Universities, about learning in the streets of Kazan rather than at college.
explanation.definitionFit: Gorky called his hard schooling his own in a book title, and colleges granting degrees are seats of learning.

clue.text: Poet of divine vision

parts.note: points to the Irish mystic poet known as AE, whose collection was titled The Divine Vision

explanation.walkthrough: George William Russell, who signed himself AE, published The Divine Vision in 1904.
explanation.definitionFit: The Irish poet and mystic George William Russell wrote a volume of verse of that name.

clue.text: His law I break in language

indicators.note: the letters of 'His law I' are broken up and reassembled

explanation.surface: Someone vows to break his law in speech.
explanation.walkthrough: 'break' rearranges HISLAWI.
explanation.definitionFit: This Bantu tongue is a lingua franca across East Africa.

clue.text: One of John Wilson's cozeners?

parts.note: refers to the Restoration playwright John Wilson's comedy The ..., peopled with tricksters

explanation.walkthrough: John Wilson's 1663 comedy The Cheats is the source; 'cozener' is an old word for a swindler.
explanation.definitionFit: A cozener is a swindler or trickster, one of the characters in the play's title.

clue.text: Sansom's dolly is after this jam

definitions.text: Sansom's dolly is after this jam

parts.words: Sansom's dolly is after this jam
parts.note: alludes to a William Sansom story in which a little girl's doll is drawn to an orange preserve

explanation.walkthrough: The jam meant is the bitter orange preserve eaten at British breakfast tables.
explanation.definitionFit: A preserve of Seville oranges is the jam spread on breakfast toast in Britain.

clue.text: Hope-inspired, romantic setting

parts.note: refers to the imaginary Central European kingdom invented by Anthony Hope for The Prisoner of Zenda

explanation.walkthrough: 'Hope' looks like the feeling, but it is the novelist Anthony Hope.
explanation.definitionFit: Anthony Hope set his swashbuckling romances in this fictional kingdom.

clue.text: One of 26s freebooters

parts.note: refers to Edith Wharton's last, unfinished novel The ..., about American heiresses in England

explanation.walkthrough: Wharton's posthumous novel The Buccaneers named its heroines after pirates.
explanation.definitionFit: A freebooter is a pirate or adventurer, the title figure of Wharton's final novel.

clue.text: "My passion cannot move, nor will it lessen from today " (Tennyson)

definitions.text: "My passion cannot move, nor will it lessen from today " (Tennyson)

parts.words: My passion cannot move, nor will it lessen from today " (Tennyson
parts.note: lines from In Memoriam with one word left out, the adjective describing the poet's fixed, steadfast passion

explanation.walkthrough: In Memoriam CXXX reads 'My ___ passion cannot move, / Nor will it lessen from to-day'.
explanation.definitionFit: A passion fixed at its core and unmoving is focused on a single point, as the poem's adjective says.

clue.text: Worker protects confused Greene character from illness

indicators.note: the worker surrounds and so protects what goes inside it

parts.note: a worker ant is the standard crossword worker

indicators.note: the name of the Greene character is jumbled

parts.note: Harry Lime is the villain of Graham Greene's The Third Man

explanation.surface: A labourer shields a muddled character from Graham Greene against sickness.
explanation.walkthrough: Harry Lime is the black-marketeer of The Third Man, Graham Greene's screenplay and novella; 'confused' jumbles his surname and 'protects' puts the worker round it.
explanation.definitionFit: A minor sickness or disorder is a synonym for illness.

clue.text: Set-up to a hundred and one quotes ()

indicators.note: the turned word is added to the numerals, following them

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred
I is the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: in a down-style 'set-up' the word is read upwards, so backwards

parts.note: taken as written before it is turned

explanation.surface: A set-up adding up to a hundred and one quotations.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Set-up' reads as an arrangement, but 'up' turns the word round and 'to' attaches it after the Roman numerals. The empty brackets in the clue as held are left over from the print.
explanation.definitionFit: To cite a passage is to quote it as evidence, so cites and quotes are synonyms as verbs.

clue.text: Tear out after taxi to Isherwood film

indicators.note: the rearranged letters come after the taxi

parts.note: a cab is a taxi

indicators.note: the letters of 'Tear' are thrown out of order

explanation.surface: Someone rips something out after hailing a taxi to see a film.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tear' could be a teardrop or a rip; here 'out' scrambles its letters and 'after' puts them behind the taxi.
explanation.definitionFit: The musical film starring Liza Minnelli was based on Isherwood's Berlin stories.

clue.text: Roman king is sailor (one of five children)

parts.note: a tar is an old word for a sailor
a quin is one of quintuplets

explanation.surface: An ancient monarch turns out to be a seaman from a family of quintuplets.
explanation.definitionFit: Tarquinius Superbus was the last of the legendary kings of early Rome.

clue.text: Wife in leisurely Rattigan part

parts.note: leisurely means unhurried, slow

explanation.surface: A wife takes her time in a Rattigan role.
explanation.walkthrough: Terence Rattigan's play The Winslow Boy centres on the Winslow family.
explanation.definitionFit: Ronnie and his father Arthur are roles in Rattigan's play The Winslow Boy.

clue.text: Mrs Trollope's was Barnaby, and she later married

explanation.surface: Frances Trollope's heroine was called Barnaby and later wed.
explanation.walkthrough: Frances Trollope, the novelist's mother, wrote The Widow Barnaby and its sequel The Widow Married.
explanation.definitionFit: A bereaved wife titles both Frances Trollope novels, the second about her remarriage.

clue.text: Instrument and French stool

parts.note: a tabor is a small drum
et is French for 'and'

explanation.surface: A musical instrument and a French stool are offered together.
explanation.definitionFit: A low upholstered seat without a back is a small stool or footstool.

clue.text: Her Aida re-orchestrated for nincompoop

indicators.note: the letters of 'Her Aida' are scored afresh in a new order

explanation.surface: Someone rescores Verdi's opera and is called a fool for it.
explanation.walkthrough: 're-orchestrated' rearranges HERAIDA.
explanation.definitionFit: An empty-headed, silly person is a slang equivalent of a fool.

clue.text: Caring verse from Maxine Kumin

explanation.surface: Tender poetry by an American Pulitzer winner.
explanation.walkthrough: Maxine Kumin, the American poet, published a 1989 collection with this title.
explanation.definitionFit: Upbringing and care are what raising a child means, and the word titles a Kumin collection.

clue.text: Her life was worth a backward glance

definitions.text: Her life was worth a backward glance

parts.words: Her life was worth a backward glance
parts.note: refers to the novelist whose 1934 autobiography was titled A Backward Glance

explanation.walkthrough: The phrase sounds like a judgement on someone's life, but A Backward Glance is the American novelist's memoir.
explanation.definitionFit: The author of The Age of Innocence wrote her memoirs under that title.
